Text: $APLD Very bullish earnings call. Wes expects more than 600 MW online over the next 12 months and another 250 MW of expansion leases signed by year end. On those leases, he’s looking for rent increases ABOVE 15%, possibly with longer terms. This is mega. APLD delivered 250 MW over the past year. Now they expect to deliver more than twice that over the next year. Polaris Forge 1 (Ellendale, ND - AI factory leased to $CRWV) already has 250 MW operating of the 400 MW contracted there. A few other things stood out for me 1. About $36 billion in contracted revenue across five AI factory campuses in 3 states. Approximately $86B if all renewal options are exercised. Polaris Forge 3 (Center, ND AI factory leased to $META) , and Delta Forge 1 and 2 (Boyce, LA and Brookwood, AL AI factory leased to $META) all have the same tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler. We know that hyperscaler is $META from public records although Wes did not confirm it. 2. Construction of all 400 MW at Polaris Forge 1 and the contracted 200 MW at Polaris Forge 2 (Harwood, ND AI factory leased to $ORCL) is fully funded. The latest $1.59B PF1 financing was at 7% interest, compared with 9.25% on the earlier PF1 debt. I like seeing the borrowing costs come down as they prove they can deliver these buildings. 3. They’re working on financing PF3, DF1 and DF2 through Macquarie preferred equity and project debt, with APLD keeping majority ownership. Management sounded confident about the terms it can get with that investment-grade tenant ($META) behind the leases. Those financings still need to close. 4. Base HPC rental income in Q1 was $65.8M, up about 49% in ONE quarter. HPC net operating income was $58.8M, with an 89% margin. And most of the 1.4 GW contracted capacity still has to come online. Adjusted EBITDA was $64.4M, excluding $CHRN. Total revenue was $341.9M, up 322%, including $183.5M of tenant fit-out work. 5. APLD finished the quarter with about $2.95B in cash plus $728M in restricted cash, against roughly $6.4B of debt. More than 80% of debt principal doesn’t mature until fiscal 2031 or later. 6. Wes sees a path to roughly 2 GW operating by the end of 2028 AND 3.5 to 4 GW by the end of 2030 - the second half was NEW news. DF1 is targeting initial operations in the first half of 2027. There is a lot of construction ahead, but we’re starting to see what this company should look like in a few years. 7. APLD signed a power agreement for a planned 1,200 MW gas plant to support PF3 expansion, with deliveries expected from 2030. APLD also owns about 10% of Base Electron. That could give them a lot more room to expandl in North Dakota. 8. Finland gives $APLD access to up to 1 GW of potential power, with initial availability expected in 2028. Limited upfront exposure, and they’re already talking to hyperscalers about the site. They looked at 30-40 sites before choosing this one. 9. Wes said he expects ALL of the big 4 hyperscalers will eventually lease AI factories from $APLD in North Dakota. 10. The more community opposition there is to the datacenters of APLD’s competitors the MORE valuable APLD (with its massive permitted AI factories and low community opposition) becomes. 11. Don’t overlook $CHRN. APLD owns approximately 96%. It has a planned 50 MW Microsoft deployment, and Wes says it’s on track for $1B in annual recurring revenue in 2027. He also sees potential for several hundred MW during 2027 to 28, separate from APLD’s large campuses. 12. To secure the pipeline, $APLD reserved roughly FOUR years of entire factory output from some suppliers. Wes also said the facilities are designed for 30-yyplus years of use and to accommodate changing equipment. 13. The rent increases were probably the most encouraging part of the call for me. If APLD can sign the next leases at the pricing Wes is seeking, while continuing to bring down their financing costs, I think there is a lot more upside here. The big theme of the call was APLD is executing well to turn all of that contracted revenue into real revenue. I still see this as a LONG term investment with the big payoff in 2028 when everything under contract is built and generating revenue. Not financial advice. Everyone must do their own due diligence. Text: $APLD Yes, I’ve read what’s public as part of my DD. Only the $CRWV leases have been publicly disclosed and filed with the SEC although of course they are in redacted form. The contents of the other leases have been disclosed in $APLD filings in terms of the characterizations of them. And yes, tenants CAN terminate the leases IF $APLD misses the delivery deadlines in the contracts. $CRWV and $ORCL both have that protection. There are grace periods, possible extensions and notice requirements, so missing a target date doesn’t automatically give the tenant a way out. For $CRWV’s first two leases, $APLD specifically says a qualifying delivery failure can let the tenant terminate the lease without a termination fee or further lease payments. For the remaining 150 MW building, there is a July 29, 2027 deadline for the first three halls to meet the required commencement conditions. Some of the details are redacted, so I wouldn’t pretend we can see every exception. For $ORCL, there is a cancellation right if delivery runs more than 150 days late against phased dates starting October 1, 2026. Fitch also reports an $ORCL parent guarantee and rights to terminate for chronic outages. But $ORCL’s actual agreements are not public, so I don’t know every notice requirement or exactly what $ORCL would owe when using one of those exits. For the $META projects at Delta Forge 1, Delta Forge 2 and Polaris Forge 3, I’ve read the public disclosures. I haven’t seen the actual tenant leases which are NOT available. To be clear, $APLD has never acknowledged $META as the tenant but Wells Fargo reported it, and I have reported it too from mine and other’s examinations of the publicly available filings. ￼ We know $APLD acknowledges construction-delay cancellation risk, but we don’t have those projects’ specific deadlines, exceptions or guarantee terms. I’m not going to claim I’ve reviewed clauses that haven’t been released. If a tenant simply changes its plans, that’s expensive. APLD says voluntary cancellation by the tenant requires payment of the entire remaining contract value. $CRWV’s clause is explicit: 100% of the remaining scheduled base rent, plus specified taxes, paid before the cancellation takes effect. That payment requirement is separate from its rights to terminate the lease for delivery failures, uncured $APLD defaults, major property damage or condemnation. The lease values are roughly $11B for $CRWV , $5B for $ORCL and $20.2B across the $META projects, over 15 years. Most have three optional five-year renewals; $ORCL has two. I count the roughly $36B of initial-term commitments separately from the much larger $85 billion figure that assumes every renewal gets exercised. There are also protections in the later $CRWV arrangements. Some leases moved to a subsidiary, with parent guarantees that kick in under specified circumstances. At ELN-02, if the subsidiary’s lease ends, the suspended parent lease resumes for those halls. Moving the lease into a subsidiary doesn’t, by itself, make the parent’s commitment disappear. As we all know, the KEY factor to $APLD raking in this huge pile of revenue is on time construction execution. So far, $APLD has executed its construction milestones flawlessly. There’s no guarantee $APLD will continue to do that but I’m quite optimistic given it’s spotless to date track record. $APLD already has the first 250 MW for $CRWV operating at Polaris Forge 1 and has projected completing another 600 MW within the next 12 months. These lease contracts make it expensive for tenants to change their minds, but $APLD still must finish the remaining buildings on time and keep them running as promised. I take the backlog seriously. The delivery deadlines are part of the deal too.

Text: Oracle is urging federal regulators to expedite approval of the 17.8-mile Green Chile natural gas pipeline, warning that delays threaten its massive Project Jupiter data center campus in New Mexico. The project’s operational target has slipped to February 2027 from August after local opposition forced Transwestern Pipeline, a subsidiary of Energy Transfer, to reroute the pipeline onto federal land. Environmental groups and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez are pressing FERC to assess the combined environmental impact of the pipeline and data center before granting final approval. Stocks have historically done best in the year after the midterms. Washington Trust Bank looked at 1979 through 2023 and found that stocks in big U.S. companies returned an average of 20% that year, including dividends. The averages for the other years were 16.6% in a president’s first year, 4.7% in the midterm year, and 7.1% in the presidential election year. So the year after midterms came out ahead of all three. https://www.watrust.com/articles/understanding-us-market-returns-in-presidential-election-years Capital Group looked further back, to 1950, and found a similar result. The S&P 500 gained an average of 15.1% in the 12 months after midterm elections. That was almost twice the average gain over similar periods in other years. These are two different ways of measuring returns, but both show that stocks have tended to do well after midterms. https://www.capitalgroup.com/advisor/insights/articles/midterm-elections-markets-5-charts.html The gains have often started before the election year ends. A study in The Journal of Wealth Management found especially strong returns in the last three months of the midterm year and the first six months of the next year. This time around, that means October 2026 through June 2027. That doesn’t mean we’ll get the same result this time. Text: AI stocks rebounded Monday, but debt risks remain a major concern. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1%. Oracle ($ORCL) rose 1%, Intel ($INTC) gained 2.4%, AMD ($AMD) climbed 1.8% and Micron Technology ($MU) added 3%. CoreWeave ($CRWV) closed fractionally lower after hitting a 52-week low. The bond market tells a more troubling story. CoreWeave’s 9.625% bond due in 2032 yielded 14.9%, while its five-year credit default swap spread stood near 1,082 basis points—a distressed level signaling serious credit concerns. Oracle faces scrutiny, too. S&P rates it BBB-, the lowest investment-grade rating; Fitch rates it BBB and Moody’s Baa2. Oracle’s five-year credit default swap spread reached 315 basis points Monday, up 311% year over year, according to CNBC. The takeaway: AI demand is strong, but financing its infrastructure carries growing risks. Watch debt costs, refinancing needs and cash flow. A downgrade of Oracle to junk status could signal broader credit contagion across the AI trade. (CNBC)
